title: Weekly Deep Dive: Is United About to Buy JetBlue?
summary: JetBlue's stock has cratered to all-time lows, creditors have brought in bankruptcy lawyers, and United's CEO is already talking about "the deal of a generation." Ryan and Hope dig into whether this is really the first big airline acquisition in over a decade, what United would actually be buying, and why antitrust regulators already killed a smaller version of this exact deal.

topic.topic: JetBlue's financial collapse is creating a once-in-a-decade acquisition opportunity for United Airlines, with major implications for industry consolidation and competition.
topic.why: JetBlue's stock has plummeted to all-time lows, creditors have hired bankruptcy advisors, and frequent flyer debt trades at 42 cents on the dollar—creating conditions for United to potentially acquire a major carrier at distressed valuations. This represents the first genuine consolidation threat since the 2010s and could reshape Northeast corridor competition.
key_facts: JetBlue stock fell below $3 with creditors hiring restructuring experts amid $2 billion in frequent flyer debt valued at 42 cents on the dollar
United CEO Scott Kirby has publicly discussed JetBlue as a potential 'deal of a generation' acquisition target
JetBlue has added free first-class upgrades and loyalty perks in recent weeks, signaling desperation to retain revenue and market position
The carrier controls valuable Northeast infrastructure and Caribbean routes that would be highly attractive to a consolidator
JetBlue was already losing market share to premium-focused competitors before financial deterioration accelerated

angles: What would a United-JetBlue merger mean for Northeast competition—would it eliminate the only premium-focused carrier offering direct competition to American and Delta in Boston and New York?
How would regulatory approval work—would DOJ block this as anticompetitive consolidation, or view it as financial rescue?
What's the timeline—is JetBlue weeks away from Chapter 11, or months? How desperate are creditors to force a sale rather than restructure?
How would loyal JetBlue customers be affected—would their frequent flyer miles transfer to United, and at what value?
Could other buyers emerge—would Southwest, Alaska, or even a private equity consortium bid to keep competition alive?
